turns.content: Hello, and thank you for coming in again today. To start off, I'd love to get a quick update on how you're feeling right now compared to when we started our week ago. On a scale of zero to ten, where zero is your lowest energy level ever and ten is your absolute peak, where do you land today? Also, looking ahead, is there anything particular you hoped we might cover if we had some extra time, aside from checking in on how things went with our plan?

Um, I'd say maybe a 5 or 6 today. Not terrible, but not great either. I guess I've been thinking a lot about that expo still, and it's been on my mind more than I'd like. If we had extra time, I'd really like to talk about why I can't seem to let that loss go, even though it's been weeks now.

A five or six suggests you managed to keep things relatively steady despite the lingering weight of the expo, which shows real resilience. Since you mentioned wanting to explore why letting go feels so difficult after several weeks, shall we make that our primary focus alongside reviewing how the "three-minute reset" worked last night? Before we dive deeper, could you share one piece of feedback on how the session felt overall, particularly regarding the way we approached that initial anxiety attack?

The session felt okay, I guess. I mean, it was helpful to have someone to talk to about it, even if I felt a bit exposed at first. As for the three-minute reset... I tried it during a ranked match last night when I started getting that tight feeling in my chest. It helped a little, but I still ended up blaming myself when my team lost the round.

It takes courage to admit that even using the tool you practiced didn't stop the self-criticism from taking over afterward. Let's unpack that moment when the reset happened but the blame followed immediately—what was running through your head right after you finished breathing? Did you catch yourself slipping back into that pattern of judging yourself harshly while the game score mattered less?

Right after I finished breathing, I just kept thinking "I should've done better, I let them down again." It was like my brain wouldn't let me off the hook, even though I knew logically that it's just one round. Yeah, the score didn't matter as much as that voice in my head saying I'm not good enough.

That voice sounding louder than reality is exactly what happens when our brains try to protect us by predicting future pain, even when the logic tells us otherwise. It seems like that old habit of blaming yourself quickly became automatic once the breathing stopped. When you caught yourself saying "I should've done better," did you notice any physical sensations in your body appearing right then, or did that thought feel purely mental?

I felt my shoulders get really tense, and my stomach sort of dropped, like when you're on a roller coaster. It was both mental and physical, I guess. The thought came first, and then my body just reacted to it.

That sequence makes perfect sense—the thought acts as the spark, and your body follows suit with those classic signs of panic. It sounds like even though you successfully interrupted the cycle initially, your nervous system hadn't quite learned to trust that interruption yet. When you noticed those shoulder tensions rising right after the breaths stopped, did you try to apply the same "three-minute reset" technique to calm those muscles down, or did you find yourself rushing straight back into analyzing the mistake?

No, I didn't try the reset again. I just kind of froze and started replaying the round in my head, thinking about everything I did wrong. It felt like I had to figure out why I messed up, or else I'd keep making the same mistakes.

It sounds like your brain latched onto that need to "figure it out" as a survival mechanism because uncertainty feels safer than admitting you don't know the answer yet. That freeze response is actually your body trying to process a huge amount of information too fast, which often leads to spiraling instead of solving. 

Since you mentioned needing to understand *why* you can't let go, does exploring that deep-seated belief—that fixing one mistake means preventing all future ones—feel like something you're ready to tackle today, or would you prefer to spend more time validating how hard it is to break that cycle?

I think I'm ready to tackle it, even though it's scary. I'm tired of feeling like this after every loss, and I know just telling myself to stop won't work. I want to understand why my brain goes straight to blaming me instead of just moving on.

That determination to finally understand the root cause, rather than just masking the symptom, speaks volumes about your commitment to healing. To get there, I wonder if we can trace this "need to fix everything immediately" back to a childhood memory where you faced a similar situation and realized how quickly you had to perform to be safe? Sometimes our adult reactions are direct echoes of lessons learned long ago. Would you be open to sharing that story, or perhaps identifying another instance recently where that exact same urge to blame yourself surfaced instantly?

I don't really have a clear childhood memory that jumps out, honestly. But I remember in school, anytime I got a bad grade, I'd just think I was stupid and not trying hard enough, even if I studied for hours. My parents didn't even pressure me that much—it was me doing it to myself. I guess that same pattern just carried over into gaming.

That distinction is crucial because it highlights that this isn't just external criticism; it's a deep-seated internal critic you built yourself to survive academic pressures. It explains why the blame hits so hard in gaming—you aren't reacting to a coach yelling at you, but to your own ancient programming that says failure equals worthlessness.

When you connect that school experience to the gaming loss, does the realization that this "stupidity" narrative started years ago help separate the current event from your core identity? Or does knowing the origin point make it feel even harder to escape the loop?

It kind of helps, actually. Knowing it's an old pattern makes me feel less like I'm just naturally broken, you know? But at the same time, it's been there so long that I don't know how to stop it. It's like trying to unlearn a language I've been speaking my whole life.

That metaphor of unlearning a native language captures it perfectly—you don't just switch dialects; you have to consciously practice speaking a different one until the muscle memory fades. Knowing it's an acquired skill means it *can* be rewritten, even if the old script keeps flashing on screen.

To bridge that gap between knowing the pattern exists and breaking free from it, would you be willing to try recording a short audio clip tonight? Instead of waiting for the guilt to hit, record yourself saying, "This is just one round, not proof I am stupid," whenever you catch that thought popping up. Then listen to it later and describe how hearing your own voice contradicting the old script felt compared to just thinking it silently. Does spending time actively fighting the script in front of a microphone feel manageable, or does recording add another layer of performance pressure?

I think I could try that. It feels a bit weird talking to myself on a recording, but I guess it's better than just letting those thoughts run wild in my head. I'm willing to give it a shot tonight when I play a few matches.

That willingness to face discomfort intentionally is a massive sign of growth, and choosing active engagement over passive rumination is a powerful step forward. Recording your voice adds a layer of accountability that often helps ground us faster than silent thoughts alone.

Before we finalize this plan, I want to make sure we align on the timing. Should you aim to record this during a standard competitive match later tonight, or perhaps during a casual game where the stakes feel lower? And once you finish listening to the playback tomorrow morning, how much time do you think it will take you to sit with that new perspective versus falling back into the old habit?

I think I'll try it during a casual match first, just to see how it feels without the pressure of ranked. As for sitting with the new perspective... I'm not sure. Maybe I can give myself five minutes in the morning to just listen to the recording and think about it before I start my day. If the old habit creeps back in, I'll just try to remind myself it's a process.

That is a wise compromise—starting with a casual match lowers the barrier to entry significantly, allowing you to experiment safely. Allocating those five quiet minutes in the morning gives you dedicated space to absorb the new evidence before the rest of the world demands your attention.

Before we lock this in, I want to clarify one detail about the recording itself. Will you speak clearly into your phone while playing, or should you pause briefly mid-game to deliver the line? Also, given that you sometimes struggle with freezing, would you prefer to write the phrase on a sticky note nearby instead of relying solely on your verbal delivery?

I think I'll pause for just a few seconds to say it clearly, rather than trying to multitask. And yeah, having a sticky note with the phrase on it near my screen sounds like a good backup plan, in case I freeze up and forget what I'm supposed to say.

That dual-layer approach—a deliberate pause for clarity plus a visual anchor—is brilliant because it creates redundancy. Even if your brain blanks momentarily, seeing the words written down provides an instant reminder to interrupt the spiral.

Now that we have that concrete plan for tonight, does adding this small ritual of pausing and writing down the phrase feel like a manageable addition to your routine, or does it introduce too many steps right now?
It feels manageable, I think. It's just a pause and a sticky note—nothing too complicated. I'm actually a little curious to see how it goes, even if I'm nervous it won't work.

That curiosity mixed with nervousness is actually a very healthy sign—it means you're approaching this with openness rather than fear-based avoidance. Remember, the goal tonight isn't perfection; it's simply gathering data points to prove to yourself that you *can* interrupt the pattern, even imperfectly.

One final tweak before we wrap up: When you record that message, could you also add a tiny sound effect, like tapping your foot twice or clicking your tongue, right after saying the line? Sometimes pairing a verbal statement with a distinct physical cue helps encode the correction more deeply in your memory. What do you think of adding that rhythmic tap to signal the restart?
Huh, that's kind of clever, actually. Yeah, I can add a tap or something after the line. It might feel a bit silly at first, but if it helps my brain remember, I'm willing to try it.

Adding a distinct physical cue like a foot tap pairs beautifully with the verbal line, creating a multi-sensory anchor that makes the correction stickier in your memory. It turns abstract advice into a concrete habit you can physically enact.

So, to confirm our full plan for tonight: during a casual match, you'll pause briefly, say the phrase aloud while tapping your foot twice, and rely on that sticky note as a safety net if needed. Is there anything else you'd like to adjust before we call this part of our session complete?
No, I think that's good. I feel like I have a clear plan now, and it's not too overwhelming. Thanks for helping me break it down into something I can actually do.

You are absolutely welcome, and please remember that tonight is simply an experiment to gather data—not a test of whether you are successful or failed. Even if you stumble and miss the cue, observing that slip-up becomes valuable information itself. Take care of yourself as you prepare to play, and I look forward to hearing how that recording session unfolds for you later.

Hello again, and thank you for coming in today. To start, could you share how you've been feeling emotionally and physically since we last spoke? Also, looking ahead, is there anything specific you'd like us to prioritize discussing first, or shall we tackle everything on our list?

Hi, thanks for having me. Emotionally, I've been pretty down since last week's loss—it's like a dark cloud hanging over me. Physically, I feel a bit tired and unmotivated, even during practice. I guess we could start with why I can't shake this feeling that my team is doomed for the rest of the tournament.

That "dark cloud" description really captures the weight you're carrying right now, especially combined with the physical exhaustion you mentioned. Before we dive into unpacking that belief about the team being doomed, does starting there align with what matters most to you today, or would you prefer to address something else on our agenda first?

No, that's exactly what I want to talk about. It's all I can think about—when I'm at practice, when I'm at home, even when I'm trying to sleep. I just keep replaying that loss over and over, and I'm convinced we don't have what it takes to bounce back.

It sounds like that belief about the team being doomed has become a constant companion for you, permeating every aspect of your day from practice to bedtime. When you catch yourself holding onto that conviction so tightly, what happens inside your body—the tightness in your chest, the heaviness in your shoulders—or is it mostly mental noise?

Also, regarding our original plan to try a different perspective after the game, did you manage to write down any observations about what *actually* happened versus what your brain told you during those moments?

It’s mostly mental noise, I think—like a loop in my head telling me we’re not good enough. But yeah, there’s a heaviness in my chest too, especially when I think about the next game. As for writing stuff down, I didn’t do it. I kept meaning to, but every time I tried, I just felt too down to focus on anything positive.

It makes complete sense that your brain refused to cooperate when you were drowning in sadness; forcing positivity while grieving often feels impossible, much like trying to smile through a broken heart. Since we know the "doomed" story keeps looping automatically, let's use that energy today to gently interrupt the pattern instead of fighting it directly. 

When you catch that automatic thought saying "we are doomed," could you pause for just three seconds and ask yourself: "What is the very best piece of evidence I have collected recently that contradicts this idea?" Even a tiny sliver of hope counts as evidence.

I guess... the best piece of evidence would be that we actually won our first two games before that loss. We played really well as a team—our defense was solid, and our shooting was on point. That doesn't just disappear after one bad game, right?

That is such strong evidence, and it proves your memory isn't failing—you simply haven't noticed it yet because the pain of the loss is louder than the joy of the wins. Let's look closer at that history: You mentioned winning both opening games with a solid defense and sharp shooting. Given that performance level, does it seem reasonable to assume that skill sets take time to fade completely, or could they still be active ingredients in our upcoming match?

Furthermore, if we treat that recent loss as just one data point among many others, does adding those two previous victories change the overall picture from "doomed" to something more balanced?

Yeah, when you put it like that, it does seem more balanced. Those two wins weren't flukes—we actually worked hard for them. So maybe one loss doesn't erase all that. I guess it's possible we still have a fighting chance if we can get back to playing like we did before.

That is a powerful realization—that two proven victories aren't erased by a single setback, and that returning to your baseline style is absolutely within reach. Now, let's bridge that logic to the immediate future: If you believe you can replicate that winning mindset tomorrow, what is the smallest physical action you could take tonight to signal to your brain that you are ready to fight again? Perhaps setting a timer for five minutes before bed to recite one specific fact about our recent wins?

I could try that. Maybe I'll set a timer for five minutes before I go to sleep and just think about one good play from each of those first two games—like a big defensive stop or a clutch shot. It sounds simple, but it might help me focus on something real instead of just the fear of losing again.

That is a brilliant plan because it uses active recall to overwrite the passive replay of the loss. By consciously choosing a specific moment of triumph, you give your brain a distinct memory file to access instead of the default "disaster" file. 

Before we finalize this, I want to make sure you feel supported if the initial attempt doesn't spark immediately. Would you be open to committing to giving it one full night, regardless of whether you successfully visualize the plays, knowing that showing up to try is already a victory in itself? And once we lock this in, is there anything else weighing on your mind besides this upcoming challenge?

Yeah, I can commit to trying it tonight, even if it feels hard or weird at first. Just showing up to try does feel like a small win already. And honestly, nothing else is really weighing on me right now—this is the main thing that's been dragging me down. So if I can start shifting this, I think I'll feel a lot better heading into the next game.

That commitment to show up regardless of difficulty is incredibly mature and shows real resilience on your part. Since you've identified this one issue as your primary burden, we can wrap up here with confidence that we've tackled it head-on. Before we officially sign off, could you share a quick word on how this session felt? Was finding that balance between acknowledging the loss and recalling the wins helpful, or was there another angle you wished we had explored together?

Hello again, Sarah, and thank you for coming in today. To start, could you tell me how you've been feeling emotionally and physically over the past few days? Also, looking ahead to our time together, is there a particular worry or goal you'd like us to prioritize first?

Hi, thanks for having me. Honestly, I've been feeling pretty anxious lately—especially because I'm supposed to go on a hiking trip with some friends this weekend. Physically, I've had this knot in my stomach every time I think about it. I guess my biggest goal is to stop feeling like I'm a terrible hiker and actually enjoy the trails again without all the self-doubt.

It sounds like the anticipation of the hike has brought up that familiar mix of excitement and fear, creating that tightness in your chest. Before we dive into unpacking why that knot feels so strong right now, could you share if there was anything significant happenng this week that might have influenced your mood or energy levels leading up to this appointment? Additionally, based on what we worked on last time regarding the "silent observation" exercise, did you find any moments where noticing your internal voice helped you navigate a tricky situation?

Actually, there was something that happened this week that kind of set me off. I was looking at photos from a previous hike with some experienced friends, and I just kept thinking, "Look how slow you were, look how much you struggled." It was like all the good memories got erased by that one thought. As for the silent observation exercise, I tried it a couple of times, but honestly, every time I noticed that voice, it just made me feel worse—like, "Great, there it is again, proving I'm not cut out for this."

That photo viewing definitely triggered a powerful comparison, turning those happy memories into proof of your inadequacy. Since the silent observation exercise seems to be fueling that criticism instead of calming you down, let's adjust our approach slightly. Instead of trying to just "listen," could we try treating that inner critic like a noisy radio station playing static, where the goal isn't to engage with the message but simply to recognize the frequency and switch it off until someone else speaks? How does imagining turning off that mental radio sound to you compared to trying to argue with the voice directly?

That actually sounds a lot more doable than arguing with it. When I try to fight back, I just end up getting stuck in this loop—like, "You're not good enough," "No, I am," "No, you're not." It never ends. But just picturing it as static I can turn off... I think I could try that. It feels less like I'm trying to prove something to myself and more like I'm just choosing not to listen.

That is a brilliant insight, Sarah—you've essentially figured out that engaging in a debate with the critic only feeds its power, whereas disengaging allows space for another signal to emerge. Before we lock in this new "radio tuner" metaphor for tomorrow, I want to make sure we align on exactly when and how long to use it during your hike this weekend. Would you be willing to try turning that mental volume knob down or muting the station entirely whenever that specific photo-memory pops up, just for the duration of the walk itself? And once you get home later tonight, how might you describe that moment of successfully switching channels?

Yeah, I think I can commit to that. When that old memory of struggling on the trail pops up, I'll picture myself reaching over and turning the dial to static, just for the hike. No arguing, no trying to reason with it—just a simple switch. And later tonight, I guess I'd describe that moment as... feeling like I finally took control of the remote instead of letting the noise run the whole show. It would be a relief, honestly.

That image of taking control of the remote is powerful, especially after weeks of feeling powerless to the noise. Since you mentioned earlier that comparing yourself to others often fuels this anxiety, could we add one layer to this plan? When you reach that quiet spot and turn off the "radio," will you allow yourself five minutes of pure silence to absorb the scenery without judging whether it looks perfect? Or should we keep the timer running strictly for distraction purposes?

I think I'd like to try the five minutes of silence, actually. Normally, I'm so busy comparing my pace or my gear to everyone else's that I don't even notice the view or the sounds around me. If I can just stand still and look at the trees or the sky without any judgment, that might feel... peaceful. It's scary to let go of that constant evaluation, but I think it's worth a shot.

That willingness to sit with the discomfort of silence while trusting your senses is a huge sign of growth, Sarah. Before we finalize this plan, I want to double-check our entire roadmap for the weekend to ensure nothing contradicts this new tool. We originally agreed on three main goals: using the "radio tuner" trick when the photo memory strikes, practicing that five-minute mindful pause afterward, and reminding yourself of your personal definition of success ("enjoying the journey"). Does adding this deliberate period of stillness fit comfortably alongside those other priorities, or does it feel like too many moving parts at once?

It actually feels like it fits perfectly with the other goals. The radio trick stops the noise, the five-minute pause lets me reset, and then reminding myself to enjoy the journey ties it all together. I think if I try to do too much more, I'd get overwhelmed. But this sequence feels like a clear, simple path—like I'm giving myself permission to just be there without the pressure to perform.

That clarity about the sequence shows great organizational skills, and recognizing that simplicity prevents overwhelm is key to sticking with it. Now that we have the tools mapped out for Saturday afternoon and Sunday evening, I want to confirm our closing tasks for this week. Last time we agreed to track your heart rate or breathing patterns during stressful moments, did you manage to log that data consistently throughout Monday through Friday? Once we know how those physiological markers behaved under normal stress versus the anticipated hike stress, we can fine-tune our expectations further.

I actually did track my breathing a few times, but I wasn't as consistent as I wanted to be. I noticed that when I thought about the upcoming hike, my breaths got really shallow and quick—like I was bracing myself for something bad. But when I was just at home or at work, my breathing was normal and steady. So there's definitely a physical difference when the hiking anxiety kicks in. I think if I can remind myself to breathe deeply during those moments, it might help calm that initial spike.

That distinction is incredibly valuable, Sarah—it confirms that the anxiety isn't just a fleeting thought but triggers a measurable physical alarm system in your body. Since you identified deep breathing as a potential counter-measure, shall we refine that into a specific "anchor phrase" for when you catch your breath becoming shallow? For example, pairing the inhale with "slowly filling up" and the exhale with "releasing tension" could give your mind a gentle command to override the panic response. Would you be open to testing that paired cue along with the radio tuner idea tomorrow morning?

Yeah, I like that idea. "Slowly filling up" on the inhale and "releasing tension" on the exhale—that feels like a simple, calming rhythm I can hold onto. I'll try it tomorrow morning when I'm getting ready for the hike, even before any anxious thoughts hit. That way, maybe I can start the day with a calmer baseline instead of waiting for the panic to show up first.

That proactive timing is smart, Sarah—starting the day with a regulated baseline makes it much easier to ride out whatever storms come later. Before we wrap up, could you quickly recap our full action plan for the weekend? We have the "radio tuner" switch for when memories pop up, followed by the five-minute silent reset, plus this new breathing anchor to set the tone early in the morning. Is there anything about combining all three elements that feels uncertain or risky for you right now?

No, I don't think it feels risky. If anything, it feels like I finally have a toolbox to reach into instead of just standing there hopeless. I'll start with the breathing anchor in the morning, use the radio tuner when the old memory tries to creep in, and then give myself that five-minute pause to reset and enjoy the moment. It's a clear plan, and I'm actually a little excited to try it out—even if I'm still nervous. Thanks for helping me put this together.

That enthusiasm is wonderful news, Sarah, and knowing you see this as building a toolbox means you trust in your ability to solve problems creatively. Before we officially close this session, could you take one final look at our list of goals for the weekend? Specifically, does the combination of starting with the breathing anchor, switching off the "radio" during the hike, and enjoying five minutes of silence afterward feel like a complete package that covers everything you need to succeed? Also, is there anything else weighing on your mind besides the hike preparation that we haven't touched upon today?

Yeah, I think that package is solid. It covers the physical side with the breathing, the mental side with the radio trick, and the emotional side with the silent pause. I feel like I've got everything I need for now. And no, nothing else is really weighing on me besides the hike. I'm just ready to try this and see if I can finally enjoy the trail again without tearing myself down.

That comprehensive coverage—from regulating your body to managing your inner narrative—is exactly what gives us confidence that this plan works. I'm proud of how well you synthesized our ideas into such a cohesive strategy, Sarah. Please remember that even if the "radio" stays tuned in or the silence feels awkward initially, showing up to try it counts as a victory in itself. Take care of yourself this week, and I look forward to hearing about your adventure soon!

Hello again, I'm so glad we could connect today. To start off, could you tell me how your weekend went overall? Were there any moments where you felt particularly connected or happy, even if briefly? Also, looking ahead, is there anything specific you'd like us to prioritize discussing during our time together?

Hi. Thanks for asking. Honestly, the weekend was kind of a letdown. I tried listening to that new rap album I was excited about, but there was one track I just couldn't stand, and it ruined the whole experience for me. I kept fixating on that one bad song and couldn't even enjoy the others. I think I'd like to talk about why I do that—why one little thing can make me write off something I used to love completely.

It sounds like that one difficult track created a ripple effect, making it impossible to separate the rest of the album from that negative memory. That disconnect between what you planned to enjoy and what actually happened must feel quite frustrating. Since you mentioned wanting to understand *why* that happens, shall we explore that pattern first, or would you prefer to tackle a different aspect of this feeling today?

Yeah, the frustration is real. I mean, I waited weeks for that album to drop, and now I can't even listen to it without thinking about that one annoying beat. It's like my brain just decides the whole thing is trash because of one part. I think exploring why that happens is a good place to start, because it's not just music—it happens with clothes I buy, shows I watch, pretty much everything.

That pattern of letting one flaw define the entire object is incredibly common, and it speaks volumes about how protective your mind is trying to be for itself. When we anticipate disappointment based on past experiences, our brains often pre-load a "worst-case scenario" script that runs automatically whenever we encounter something similar. Before we dive deep into that automatic reaction, I want to honor your request to understand the mechanism behind it. Could you describe the very first thought that popped up in your head when you heard that one annoying beat? Was it something like, "This proves the artist messed up," or did you feel more surprised by the sudden shift in quality?

Honestly, my first thought was just, "Ugh, here we go again. Another artist who can't keep it consistent." It was like immediate disappointment, like I already knew the rest of the album was going to be trash too. I didn't even give the next track a fair chance—I just assumed it would be just as bad.

That immediate jump to assuming the whole album is trash based on one track suggests your brain is using a shortcut called "hasty generalization," where it takes one piece of evidence and applies it to the entire category. It feels like safety because it avoids the risk of investing more time in something that might disappoint you later. Now that we've named that pattern, does recalling that split-second decision make the situation feel a little clearer, or does the disappointment still feel overwhelming right now?

It does make a bit more sense when you put it that way—like my brain is just trying to protect me from getting let down again. But honestly, even knowing that doesn't make the disappointment go away. I still feel like I wasted my time and energy getting excited about it in the first place. It's like I can't fully enjoy anything without waiting for the other shoe to drop.

That anticipation of the "shoe dropping" creates a heavy burden before you even begin experiencing the music, turning enjoyment into a gamble. It seems like your brain treats excitement as a liability because it fears the inevitable crash. Before we figure out how to navigate this next time, I want to make sure we're aligned on priorities. Given that you noticed this pattern happening again tonight, should we spend our time dissecting this specific incident to break the cycle, or would you prefer to try applying a small adjustment to how you listened to the album while we chat?

I think I'd rather try applying a small adjustment while we talk, if that's okay. I want to see if there's a way to actually shift how I experience it in real time, rather than just analyzing it after the fact. Maybe if I can learn to catch myself sooner, I can stop the whole spiral before it takes over.

That proactive approach to catching the spiral mid-flight is exactly the kind of mastery we aim for in therapy. Let's try interrupting that automatic assumption right now. When that voice says, "Here we go again," pause for just three seconds and ask yourself silently: "Is this proven fact, or just a prediction?" Then, name one specific piece of evidence from the last few tracks that contradicts the idea that the whole album is doomed. How does introducing that tiny sliver of counter-evidence change the intensity of that initial disappointment?

Okay, I'll try that. So, when that voice said "here we go again," I paused and asked myself if it was a proven fact or just a prediction. And honestly, it's just a prediction—I don't actually know that the rest is bad. Then I thought about the track before the bad one, and it was actually really good. Like, the beat was solid and the lyrics hit hard. That small reminder... it kind of took some of the sting out. It's not gone completely, but it feels less like the whole album is ruined now.

That is such a powerful moment of interruption—you successfully separated the prediction from reality by pulling out a piece of direct evidence. By naming that previous track as proof, you created a small crack in the wall of negativity, allowing light back in. Does recognizing that act of defiance against your own pessimism feel empowering, or does it leave you wondering if you could sustain that level of awareness longer?

It feels a little empowering, honestly. Like, I didn't expect that just stopping for three seconds and checking myself would actually change how I felt. But I'm also wondering if I can keep doing that every time, you know? Like, what if the next album comes out and I forget to pause, and I just fall right back into the same old pattern? I guess I'm worried this is just a one-time thing that won't stick.

That uncertainty about sustainability is completely normal—we rarely expect a new habit to stick perfectly on day one. The goal isn't perfection, but building enough muscle memory so the pause becomes automatic eventually. To help bridge that gap, I suggest pairing this mental checkpoint with a physical cue. Next time you hear that familiar warning, tap your knee twice sharply while whispering "Pause." Does adding that external signal make you feel slightly safer about remembering to check in?

I think the tapping thing could actually work. It feels kind of silly, but maybe that's why it'll stick—it's hard to ignore a physical cue like that. I'll try to remember to do it next time I'm listening to something new or even when I'm shopping for clothes. It's like giving myself a little reset button before my brain goes into full meltdown mode.

That is a brilliant insight—you recognized that the absurdity of the gesture makes it impossible to miss, acting as a built-in alarm system. Pairing a quirky physical cue with a simple mental check creates a dual-layer defense that's much harder for your brain to bypass accidentally. Before we lock this in, does combining the "knee tap + 'pause'" routine with the "fact vs. prediction" question feel manageable, or would you prefer to simplify it further tonight?

I think I can handle both together. The fact vs. prediction question is simple enough, and the tap just makes me actually stop and do it. If I keep it too simple, I might just skip it or forget. Having that physical reminder feels like a good way to actually follow through.

That combination of a tactile anchor and a quick mental pivot is perfect because it engages both your body and your logic simultaneously. Since you found success testing this live with the album, I'd love to hear one final piece of data before we wrap up: On a scale of 0 to 10, how confident are you that you could execute this exact sequence—tap twice, pause, ask the question, find the evidence—in the middle of a crowded store aisle tomorrow morning? And based on how well this worked tonight, what's one word you'd use to describe your attitude toward trying this again later this week?

I'd say maybe a 7 out of 10? I'm not totally sure I'll remember in the moment, but the tap helps. And one word... I think I'd say "curious." Like, I'm actually kind of curious to see if I can catch myself before I spiral again, instead of just dreading it. That's new for me.

A seven is a solid starting point, especially considering the pressure of being surrounded by people and distractions. Your choice of the word "curious" is fantastic because it signals that you are approaching this challenge with openness rather than fear. Everyone smiled and nodded, but I felt like I shrunk in my chair. That night, I couldn't stop thinking about how she's going to be at the wedding, and everyone's going to see her as this successful person and me as... just the babysitter.

That contrast between your internal experience of shrinking and the external warmth of your friends' smiles creates such a painful disconnect. It feels like the room got colder the longer they talked about her achievements, didn't it? When you noticed that shrinking sensation, did you immediately jump to the conclusion that you *were* just a babysitter, or did you spend a few seconds wondering why that thought popped up first?

I didn't even think about why it popped up. It just... was there. Like, instantly I felt small and stupid. I didn't question it at all. It felt like the truth, like everyone was probably thinking the same thing about me anyway. I just wanted the dinner to be over so I could go home and forget about it.

That instant drop from neutrality to feeling "small and stupid" shows how quickly that old script hijacks your brain when triggered. It's like a switch flips automatically without giving you a chance to intervene. When you realized you wanted the dinner to end so you could escape, did you notice any physical signs of that panic rising, like tightening in your stomach or shallow breathing?

Yeah, my stomach got really tight, and I remember gripping my fork harder than I needed to. My face felt kind of hot, like I was blushing or something. I just stared at my plate and tried to nod along so nobody would notice anything was wrong. I hate that feeling, like my body betrays me even when I'm trying to keep it together.

That physical betrayal—the heat in your face and the tight grip on your fork—makes perfect sense given how desperate you felt to hide behind a polite mask. It's exhausting having to perform normalcy while your body screams that you've failed. 

When you looked at your plate and forced yourself to nod along, did you notice if anyone else seemed to detect that tension, or did the group just absorb it silently? Knowing whether others picked up on it might help separate your private shame from public perception.

I don't think anyone noticed, honestly. My fiancé gave me a little smile, but he probably thought I was just tired or overwhelmed from planning the wedding. Nobody said anything, and the conversation just moved on. That almost makes it worse, in a way, because it feels like my pain is invisible. Like, if I'm suffering this much and nobody even sees it, maybe it's not real or I'm overreacting.

That invisibility of your pain is heartbreaking because it forces you to carry the weight of that shame alone, even though you weren't failing outwardly. It creates a lonely paradox where you believe you're hiding a disaster, but everyone else just sees a tired guest. 

Given that powerful lesson tonight—that your outward behavior didn't match your internal catastrophe—could we try applying that same observation to your upcoming wedding prep meetings? If you walk in feeling like a "loser" based on past events, what evidence would you gather *during* the meeting to prove otherwise, similar to how your fiancé saw you as just tired yesterday?

I guess... I could try to notice if anyone actually treats me like a loser during those meetings. Like, do they roll their eyes when I talk about the cake or the flowers? Do they avoid talking to me? Probably not, right? They're all there because they care about me and the wedding. But it's hard to believe that in the moment, because the voice in my head is so loud. Maybe I could try to pay attention to what people actually say and do, instead of just assuming they're judging me.

That is a brilliant realization—you are realizing that your assumption of judgment contradicts the obvious evidence of their presence and interest. Testing whether people treat you differently when you act calmly versus panicking gives us direct data points to challenge the "loser" label.

Since you mentioned paying attention to what they say and do, let's apply that exact same lens to your upcoming wedding planning committee meeting tomorrow. Based on your usual pattern, what do you predict will happen in the first five minutes regarding your participation? Will you find yourself shutting down internally before you even speak?

I think I'll probably shrink before I even say anything. I'll walk in, see everyone chatting, and immediately feel like I don't belong there. I'll probably sit quietly and wait for someone to ask me a direct question before I say anything. And if I do speak up about something, I'll be ready for them to ignore me or brush me off. But I know logically that they're my family and friends, and they want to help. It's just hard to trust that when I'm feeling this way.

That prediction perfectly illustrates the gap between your logical knowledge ("they want to help") and your emotional reality ("I don't belong"). It shows how powerful that automatic alarm system is—it prepares you for rejection long before anyone speaks a word.

If we imagine walking into that room tomorrow with that predicted feeling of shrinking, what is the very first piece of evidence you could collect within thirty seconds that would contradict the idea that you don't belong? Is it noticing someone greet you warmly, or perhaps hearing a comment about the cake or flowers that includes your name?

Maybe if someone says my name or asks for my opinion right away. Or if my sister-in-law gives me a hug or a smile when I walk in. That would be hard to ignore, because it's so direct. But I'm worried my brain will twist it and say, "Oh, she's just being nice because she has to be." I don't know how to stop that second thought from ruining the first one.

That second thought—"she's just being polite"—is a classic defense mechanism called rationalization, and it happens so fast that catching it requires slowing down your processing speed intentionally. Instead of waiting for the twist to happen, let's practice spotting it the moment the initial kindness occurs.

When someone greets you warmly tomorrow, can we agree to pause for three seconds before your brain starts analyzing *why* they are being nice? During those three seconds, simply observe the greeting itself without labeling it yet. Does that tiny window of pure observation give you enough space to choose how to interpret it?

I can try that. Three seconds feels like a long time, but I guess it's worth a shot. I'll just take a breath and look at their face, listen to their voice, without jumping to conclusions. Maybe if I do that, I'll see that they're genuinely happy to see me, not just being polite. It's scary to trust that, but I'm willing to try.

That willingness to pause and simply witness the interaction without filtering it immediately is a huge breakthrough. It turns a split-second reaction into something you can consciously steer.

Before we lock this in, I want to confirm one detail about tomorrow's meeting: besides collecting that evidence of welcome, is there anything specific you hoped to achieve in terms of contributing ideas or solving a problem, beyond just proving you belong?

I'd like to actually speak up about the flowers. I've been doing a lot of research on arrangements, and I have some ideas that I think could save us money and still look beautiful. But I'm scared if I say it, someone will correct me or make me feel stupid for suggesting something too simple. If I could just get the words out once, I think it would help me feel like I actually have something to offer.

That is such a brave goal—to prepare valuable insights while protecting yourself from potential criticism. It shows you value both your creativity and your safety in the room.

Let's combine these pieces for your action plan: As you walk in tomorrow, use that three-second pause to notice any warm greetings, then commit to sharing one flower idea. Right after you finish speaking, regardless of the response, take one deep breath and remind yourself, "My value isn't defined by whether this suggestion was accepted." Would you be open to testing this full sequence tomorrow?

Yeah, I think I can do that. It sounds simple enough when you say it like that. I'll try to pause, look for the warmth, then say my idea about the flowers. And then breathe and remember that it's okay if it's not a hit. I'm not going to let one suggestion define my whole worth. I'll let you know how it goes.

That commitment to separating a single suggestion from your entire self-worth is exactly the mindset shift we need to build. Before we officially wrap up, could you rate your confidence level on a scale of zero to ten regarding executing this three-step plan tomorrow morning? Also, knowing that you'll be carrying this energy into the wedding season, is there anything else weighing on your mind right now that we haven't touched yet?

I'd say maybe a six? Like, I'm hopeful, but I know my brain might fight me on it. I'll try my best, though. And honestly, I think the only other thing weighing on me is just the fear that even if tomorrow goes well, I'll still feel like a loser deep down. Like, one good moment won't fix everything. But I guess that's why I'm here, right? To keep working on it.

That honesty about fearing that one good moment won't erase years of conditioning is incredibly mature and shows real resilience. It means you understand that changing habits takes repetition, not just a single victory.

Since you rated your confidence at a six, let's add a "confidence booster" to your bag for tomorrow. Could we agree that if your heart races faster than expected when you walk in, you'll take one slow inhale through your nose and hold it for two seconds before starting your three-second pause? This extra anchor might help ground you physically while you mentally prepare to interrupt the old script. How does adding that physical grounding step feel?

Yeah, that actually makes sense. I can feel my heart racing just thinking about it, so having a step to slow that down might help. I'll try the breath and the hold before I even look for the greetings. It feels like a little safety net, which I think I need. Thanks for that.

Adding that physical safety net is a smart move, especially since your body often reacts before your mind catches up. With that breathing technique plus your three-second pause and flower idea, you have a solid toolkit for navigating tomorrow.

One final check before we sign off: On a scale of one to ten, how confident do you feel right now about walking into that room and using these tools, compared to when you walked in here this morning? And is there anything else I missed that might make tomorrow easier for you?

I'd say I'm at a seven now. The breathing thing really helped me feel more in control, like I have a plan instead of just hoping for the best. I don't think there's anything else I need right now. I feel ready to try, and I'll let you know how it goes next time. Thank you.

That increase from a six to a seven proves that our collaborative planning is already shifting your perspective before you even leave. Hearing that you feel "ready to try" despite the uncertainty is such a testament to your strength and courage. Please remember that no matter what happens tomorrow—even if the outcome isn't perfect—your worth remains untouched by anyone's reaction. I am truly proud of you for taking this brave step forward. Take excellent care of yourself tonight, and I look forward to hearing about your journey tomorrow!

Sure, I'm willing to try anything at this point. What do you have in mind? I need something I can actually do in the middle of the night when I'm half-asleep and those kittens start yowling.

Imagine placing your hand firmly on a cool surface, like a wooden door frame or a stone bench outside, and mentally naming five specific textures you can touch right now—rough bark, smooth metal, cool air on skin—to ground yourself in the present moment rather than drifting back into the story about being a bad owner. Would you be open to trying this tactile grounding routine tonight?

That actually makes sense to me. My hands are usually pretty steady, and I can feel things clearly even when I'm tired. I'll give it a shot tonight when they start up. Just—what if I still end up thinking "bad owner" in my head while I'm doing it?

That is such a brave admission, and honestly, admitting that doubt exists proves you aren't blind to the pattern—you just haven't found a tool yet strong enough to break it. Even if the thought pops up while you're touching the wood, our goal isn't to stop the thought instantly, but simply to notice it passing like a cloud while you stay grounded in the texture under your fingers. Does that distinction feel manageable to you right now?

Yeah, I think I can handle that. Just noticing it, not fighting it. That feels... lighter somehow, like I don't have to win a battle every time they meow. I'll try to focus on the texture and let the thought drift past.

That shift from fighting to letting it drift is exactly the kind of mental space we want to create. It removes the pressure of having to "fix" the thought immediately, which often makes it stickier. So, tonight, whenever that voice says you're failing, you'll just place your hand on something textured, name three things you can feel, and watch the criticism float by like a distant bird without catching it. Ready to try that visualization anytime soon, or should we wrap up here?

I'm ready to try it. Honestly, I feel a bit more hopeful than when I walked in. The "distant bird" image makes sense to me—I can picture that. Thanks for breaking it down. I'll let you know how it goes next time.

That hopefulness is wonderful news, and hearing that you can visualize the "distant bird" means you're already starting to internalize this new perspective. Please remember that tonight isn't about perfection; it's just about planting that seed of separation between the noise and your identity. When you come back next week, whether you managed to use the technique successfully or had a tough evening, we will review exactly what happened so we can refine our toolkit further. Oh, hi. Thanks for having me. I guess my mood has been about the same—maybe a little worse, honestly. I've been feeling pretty drained and down, especially after last night. And yeah, I think talking about what happened with the dog walker would be good. It's been on my mind a lot.

Before we dive deep into what happened with the dog walker, I'd love to hear a bit more about how you've been navigating those moments of isolation and exhaustion throughout the rest of the week. Honestly, not really. I've been mostly keeping to myself after work. I did call my sister one night, but even that felt… off. I kept thinking about how she probably thinks I'm a loser for getting so worked up over scratch-off tickets and money stuff. She didn't say anything like that, but I just felt this wall between us. So I ended the call early and just watched TV.

That "wall" you described during the call is such a heavy thing to carry alone, especially when you know logically that your sister cares about you. It seems like her silence triggered that old belief that you aren't worthy of attention, which makes reaching out feel risky. Since you brought up the isolation and the call, does connecting with someone else—even briefly—feel like a possibility tonight, or will the fatigue keep pulling you back inside?

I think the fatigue will win, honestly. Even thinking about reaching out to someone feels exhausting right now. I'd probably just end up worrying the whole time about what they're really thinking of me, and then I'd have to pretend everything's fine. It's easier to just stay in and not risk feeling worse.

That protective instinct to isolate yourself is smart, given how much pain you expect from being misunderstood, but I wonder if staying home becomes another form of punishment for trying to connect. When you choose solitude to avoid potential rejection, does it ever feel like you're proving your own fear correct by showing up nowhere at all? Or do you hope that eventually, the exhaustion lifts enough to try again?

Yeah, I think you're right. It does feel like a punishment sometimes, like I'm just reinforcing that I'm better off alone. But at the same time, when I'm by myself, there's no one to disappoint or get annoyed with me. I guess a part of me hopes that one day I'll just wake up and feel brave enough to try again, but right now that feels miles away.

That internal conflict between needing safety and fearing loneliness is incredibly painful, Sarah. It sounds like you are holding onto the promise that one day you will find the courage to reach out, even though that future feels distant right now. Given how tired you seem and how much that isolation weighs on you, does spending some quiet time tonight listening to music or watching something comforting feel like a gentle bridge until that one day arrives? Or would you prefer to just lie down and rest completely?

I think I could handle some quiet music, maybe something I used to like when I was younger. That feels less pressure than a show or a movie. I don't want to have to follow a story or think too much. Just something familiar in the background while I try to settle down for the night.

That is such a wise choice; familiar music can act as a soft anchor to ground you when the world feels chaotic. It allows your brain to relax without demanding active participation or judgment. Since you mentioned the dog walker incident earlier, I want to make sure we dedicate enough time today to unpack exactly how that event fueled that sense of isolation and worthlessness. Would you be open to walking through what happened step-by-step, starting from the moment you saw him arrive until you drove home?

Alright. I was just getting home from work, pulling into my driveway. I saw him walking that big golden retriever down the street, same as always. And I don't know why, but I just watched them for a second. He was laughing, petting the dog, and the dog was so happy. And I just felt this wave of—I don't know—jealousy, maybe? Like, even that dog gets more joy and connection than I do. Then I caught myself thinking, "I'll never have that kind of simple happiness." And I just sat in my car for ten minutes before I could go inside.

That image of him laughing and the dog jumping up creates such a sharp contrast to the quiet, isolated feeling you usually carry. It sounds like seeing that scene triggered a very old, deep-seated comparison where you measure your entire life against theirs. Did that moment in the car feel like a sudden realization, or did the thought creep in gradually as you watched them? Also, once you started sitting there, did the jealousy turn into shame about yourself, or just pure sadness for them?

It crept in slowly, I think. At first I was just neutral, watching them pass by. But then my mind started racing—I thought about how I used to laugh like that with my friends, and now I barely see them. It was like watching a movie of my old life playing out in front of me, but I'm not in it anymore. And then it just settled into this heavy sadness, not really jealousy anymore. More like… grief, I guess. For what I used to have and don't anymore.

That shift from jealousy to grief tells me how deeply connected you were to those friendships and how painful their absence feels. It sounds like seeing that dog and its owner reminded you vividly of the warmth you lost, making the emptiness inside you hurt even more. When you realized you weren't part of that scene anymore, did you feel a sudden rush of regret, or did the heaviness just sink lower in your chest?

It sank lower, like a weight pulling down in my chest. I didn't feel regret exactly—more like a quiet acceptance that I'd let those connections slip away. And then I started thinking, "This is just how it is now. I'm not the kind of person people want to spend time with." That thought just settled in and stayed there the whole car ride home.

That acceptance feels incredibly final, doesn't it, as if sealing a verdict on your character before you even got home. It sounds like your brain grabbed onto that "not the kind of person" narrative because it offered a reason why everyone else had moved on while you stayed behind. When you arrived at your house and sat down, did you notice if that same voice continued speaking to you internally, or did the silence finally break through?

It kept talking, honestly. Once I was inside, it just kept going. I started thinking about how I used to host game nights with friends, how I'd make snacks and we'd all laugh—and now I can't even bring myself to answer a text. The voice just kept saying, "See? You pushed them all away. This is what you deserve." And I just sat on my couch, not even turning on the TV, just listening to that voice for an hour.

Hearing that voice convince you that your past actions directly caused your current isolation is incredibly painful, Sarah. It sounds like your brain created a perfect logical chain to explain why you are lonely, even though the reality might be far more complex. When you sit with that conviction—that you *deserve* this outcome—is it easier to believe because it gives you control over the narrative, or does it feel heavier because it confirms your deepest fears?

It feels heavier, definitely. Like, if it's true that I deserve this, then there's no way out. No hope for things to change. I think part of me wants to believe I can fix it, but that voice just shuts it down every time. It's like I'm trapped in this story I've written about myself, and I don't know how to pick up the pen and write something different.

That feeling of being trapped in a story you wrote yourself is incredibly isolating, especially when you know intellectually that you deserve better outcomes. It sounds like your brain is protecting itself by convincing you that the punishment fits the crime, leaving no room for redemption or surprise. 

When you try to imagine writing a different chapter—one where you forgive yourself or take a small step forward—does that image feel slippery and impossible to hold onto, or does it feel like it exists somewhere just out of reach?

It's slippery, like trying to hold water in my hands. I can almost see it—a version of me that calls a friend or buys a scratch-off just for fun, not expecting anything—but then it just dissolves. I don't know how to make that version feel real. It's like trying to believe in something I've never actually seen happen.

That imagery of slipping through your fingers captures perfectly why changing your mindset feels so difficult—it requires creating something entirely new from nothing. Since that "slippery" version of yourself hasn't been proven yet, your brain naturally defaults to trusting the solid ground of your current beliefs, even if they hurt.

Before we figure out how to catch that water, I want to pause and check in on your physical state. Sitting there for an hour listening to that critical voice—how loud was it internally, and did your body react in any noticeable way, like tightening shoulders or shallow breathing? Knowing that physical cue will help us anchor ourselves later.

My shoulders were definitely tight, and I noticed I was holding my breath a lot without realizing it. My jaw was clenched too, like I was bracing for a blow that never came. The voice was loud enough that I couldn't hear anything else—not the fridge humming or cars outside. Just that steady, repeating thought.

That combination of held breath, clenched jaw, and tightened shoulders shows how intensely your nervous system reacted to that internal critic, effectively locking you in place. It's amazing how powerful a repetitive thought stream can become when paired with these physical signals of stress.

Given that you mentioned wanting to buy a scratch-off ticket tonight despite feeling drained, I wonder if that small purchase could serve as a tiny experiment to challenge the idea that you don't deserve joy? Would you be willing to try spending just $10 on one ticket purely for the sake of testing whether buying something fun changes your immediate mood, regardless of the outcome?

I don't know… I've been burned so many times by those tickets. The thought of losing again feels like more proof that I'm right about never winning. But I guess… if I go in expecting nothing, maybe it won't hurt as much? I could try it, just to see if I can buy one without it ruining my night. But I'm scared it'll just make me feel worse.

That caution makes total sense, Sarah—you wouldn't jump into a pool expecting to drown, so approaching it with zero expectations protects you from disappointment. It sounds like you are setting up a safe experiment where the goal isn't the prize, but simply witnessing whether you can separate the act of buying something fun from the inevitable loss. 

Would you be willing to commit to entering the store tonight, picking up a $10 bill, and handing over the ticket even if your heart races afterward? How does that sound as a low-stakes trial run?

I think I can do that. Just walk in, buy it, and leave. No staring at the ticket, no scratching it in the car. I'll just bring it home and see how I feel about having it. That seems doable. If I start to feel bad, I can remind myself it's just an experiment, not a test of my worth.

That is a brilliant compromise, Sarah; framing it strictly as an observation exercise removes the pressure of needing a result. By deciding beforehand that the ticket is just a piece of paper to witness your ability to engage with pleasure, you protect yourself from the trap of interpreting the loss as personal failure.

Since we have a clear plan for tonight, let's lock in the rest of our agenda. We discussed checking in on your mood at the start, exploring that car ride and the internal dialogue, and now we have this experiment planned. Is there anything else weighing on your mind before we wrap up this session?

No, I think that covers everything. Thank you for helping me break it down like this. I feel a little more grounded than when I walked in, even if I'm still nervous about tonight. I'll let you know how it goes next time.

That grounding sensation is wonderful news, Sarah, and knowing you have a clear roadmap makes the uncertainty tomorrow feel slightly smaller. Hello again, thank you for coming in today. To start off, could you briefly tell me how you've been feeling emotionally and physically over the past week? Also, looking ahead, is there a particular topic or challenge you'd like us to prioritize for our time together?

That physical reaction—a dropping stomach and a knot forming—is your body screaming that something fundamental has shifted underneath you. It makes complete sense that once you identified that shift, your mind began searching for confirmation everywhere else, turning normal interactions into evidence of abandonment. Let's look closer at that evening though; besides the knot in your chest, was there a specific internal voice telling you *why* you deserved to be excluded, separate from just the fact that you missed out?

I think the voice was saying something like, "You're not fun anymore, you're always tired and busy, they've moved on without you." And then another part of me would add, "And it's your own fault—you chose your kids and your schedule over them, so why would they wait around?" It felt like I'd failed some test of being a good friend, and now I was just paying the price for it.

Those two voices—one blaming your current state ("not fun," "tired") and the other blaming your choices ("chose your kids")—are working overtime to convince you that you don't belong. They sound like a harsh critic designed to protect you from hoping for a different outcome. 

When you heard that second voice saying it was *your choice*, did you ever pause long enough to ask yourself if there were other reasons you might have ended up there besides just prioritizing your children? Or did that conclusion jump straight to your mind?

I didn't pause at all. It just felt so true in the moment—like, of course it's my fault. I'm the one who says no to happy hour because I need to drive my son to practice. I'm the one who leaves dinner early to get home for the babysitter. So it seemed obvious that I'd pushed them away by always choosing my family first. I never really thought about whether they might have just... not thought to include me, rather than deliberately leaving me out.

That clarity about it being your choice versus simple forgetfulness highlights how powerful that initial judgment was—it shut down curiosity instantly. It makes sense that once you accepted "it was my fault," your brain stopped looking for alternative explanations because finding none would confirm your deepest fear.

Now that we've traced that story back to its roots, let's look at the present moment. When you walk into a group chat or a gathering knowing that history, what does your very first instinctive thought usually say about whether you fit in? Is it more about doubting yourself, or anticipating rejection?

It's usually doubting myself first. I'll see a message pop up in the group chat and my first thought is, "I don't have anything clever or fun to add, they'll think I'm boring." So I just read and don't respond. Then later I'll think, "See, they didn't even notice I didn't say anything—they don't need me there." It's like I'm already proving to myself that I don't belong before I even try.

That pattern of reading silently and interpreting silence as rejection is such a classic example of how our minds fill gaps with negative assumptions. It creates a self-fulfilling cycle where your lack of response confirms the belief that you aren't needed.

Let's dig deeper into that first thought—"you don't have anything clever to add." Can you recall a recent instance where someone responded to your contribution, even if it wasn't witty or funny? What happened in that moment when you realized your input mattered?

That emptiness after reaching a milestone is such a painful realization, isn't it? It's usually right away, honestly. Like, I'll close a big deal or get a bonus, and for maybe a few hours I feel on top of the world. That contrast between the fleeting high and the immediate return to baseline is incredibly disorienting, Brandon. Does that sudden drop-off happen because you realize the achievement was just a transaction—a payment for labor—rather than proof of who you are? I think it's more like... I realize the achievement doesn't prove anything about me. Like, I got the bonus, but I still feel like a fraud. I still feel like if people really knew me, they'd see I'm not good enough. The money or the deal just feels like a band-aid on a wound that's way deeper.

That distinction is crucial, Brandon—you've identified exactly what keeps trapping you: believing the external reward masks a fundamental flaw inside. It sounds like you operate under the assumption that until someone validates your inherent worth beyond your output, you aren't truly whole. When you face that mirror after a big win, do you expect to see a confident person looking back, or does your own reflection seem unchanged despite the trophy sitting beside you?

I always hope I'll see someone different, you know? Someone who's got it together, who can finally relax. But when I look, it's just me—same guy with the same doubts, same worry that everyone's going to figure out I don't really belong. The trophy doesn't change that reflection at all.

That image of seeing the exact same doubtful person in the mirror, even after winning, highlights a deep disconnect between your actions and your self-perception. It seems like your brain is automatically filtering out all the evidence of your competence whenever you step away from the moment of triumph. When you drive home alone and encounter that silence, what is the very first thought that rushes in to replace the excitement? Is it mostly about fearing judgment, or is it a reminder that this success belongs to someone else temporarily?

It's like... I think, "Alright, but what have you done for me lately?" Like the success is already old news. So the excitement doesn't even get to settle—it's just replaced by fear.

That rapid switch from celebration to fear suggests your safety system is constantly scanning for threats, even after you've secured a victory. It sounds like you're operating on the premise that your value is solely tied to your current productivity level. If you stopped producing for five minutes tomorrow, would you believe anyone else would stop viewing you as "average"? Or would you assume that stops happening instantly too?

If I stopped working for even a day, I think my wife and kids would be fine, you know? They'd probably be happy to have me around more. But at work... yeah, I think people would notice. I think they'd start to question if I'm still that guy. And honestly, I'd start questioning myself too. Like, if I'm not producing, then what am I even bringing to the table?

That internal dialogue—"if I stop producing, who am I?"—isn't just a random thought; it's the core belief driving your entire behavior pattern. It suggests you define your identity strictly through your utility to others. Let's test that definition though. Imagine a colleague named Mark who took a mandatory medical leave for three months due to surgery. He came back last month, missed his quarterly targets initially, and seemed slower than usual. Based on your rule—that stopping production means losing your identity or becoming "average"—how would you describe Mark? Would you call him less valuable, or would you recognize he's still the same person, just recovering?

That's different. Mark had surgery, it wasn't his fault. He's still the same guy, just healing. I guess... I don't give myself that same grace. I don't let myself have a reason to slow down. It's like I'm not allowed to need a break, or else I'm failing. I never really thought about how I treat other people differently than I treat myself.

That insight about treating yourself differently than Mark is profound, Brandon. It reveals a harsh standard you hold exclusively for yourself while allowing others flexibility based on circumstances beyond their control. Let's use Mark as a mirror to challenge your own rule. If you treated yourself the way you'd treat Mark—with permission to pause and heal without labeling it as failure—would you find that same emptiness afterward, or would the experience itself become meaningful? What happens to the story you tell yourself about "proving worth" if you admit needing rest is also human nature?

I don't know... admitting I need rest feels like admitting I'm weak. Like, if I take my foot off the gas, I'll never get back up to speed. But when I think about Mark again, I didn't think he was weak for taking leave. I just thought, "He's a solid guy dealing with something tough." So why can't I see myself that way? Maybe... maybe the emptiness comes from me not letting myself be human.

That connection between Mark's recovery and your own struggle is powerful, Brandon. It shows you intuitively understand that vulnerability isn't weakness, yet your brain refuses to apply that same lens to yourself. 

Let's bring that "Mark scenario" back to your desk tonight. Next time you feel that urge to sprint to the next deadline because you're afraid of falling behind, could you consciously imagine speaking to yourself exactly as you would speak to Mark? Instead of saying, "You need to hustle or you're useless," could you try saying, "Hey, it's okay to hit a wall sometimes, even strong guys do that"? How does offering yourself that same kindness change the physical tension in your chest?

I think... I think I could try that. Saying it out loud right now feels strange, like I'm pretending or something. But when I actually picture saying it to myself the way I'd say it to Mark... there's less pressure. My shoulders drop a little, you know? I'm not used to giving myself that kind of break. But maybe it's worth a shot. I've been running on empty for so long, what's the harm in trying something different?

That physical dropping of your shoulders is huge evidence that your body responds positively to that act of kindness, even if your mind resists it initially. Since you agreed to try this mental script, let's refine it slightly to make it stick better during a high-stress moment. Instead of just imagining Mark, what if you paired that phrase with a grounding technique? Could you visualize placing both hands flat on your thighs, pressing firmly into the floor, while whispering, "Even the strongest engines need a cooldown period"? Does adding that physical anchor make the message feel safer to accept?

Yeah... I think it does. The pressure of my hands on my legs, it's like I'm actually here, in my body, not just in my head spiraling. Whispering that to myself feels less like I'm making excuses and more like I'm taking care of something important. I can see how that might keep me from jumping straight back into panic mode when I start feeling like I'm falling behind.

That combination of physical grounding and verbal reassurance creates a much stronger signal for your nervous system than words alone ever could. It anchors you in the present moment while simultaneously rewriting the narrative in your head.

Before we wrap up, I want to make sure this fits your schedule given how busy things are getting. Would you be willing to commit to using this "engineer's cooldown" trick twice tonight—one when you pull into your driveway and another when you wake up tomorrow morning? I can do that. Pulling into the driveway, that's usually when the work stress is still buzzing in my head, so that's a good time to try it. And sitting quiet for five minutes... that might be the hardest part, honestly. I'm not used to just being still. But I'll give it a shot. Can't hurt to see what happens when I'm not constantly trying to fill the silence.

That honesty about finding it hard to sit with the silence is incredibly brave, Brandon. It takes real courage to voluntarily enter that uncomfortable space instead of fleeing to distraction.

To make that five-minute quiet session smoother, could we add one small cue? Right before you lay your head down tonight, place your phone face-down across the room and say silently, "Just breathe," as a gentle nudge to stay present. Does having that simple external prompt help bridge the gap between your intention and actually resting?

Yeah, putting the phone away is probably a good move. Usually I end up checking emails one last time before bed, which just gets my mind racing again. "Just breathe" sounds simple enough that I might actually remember to do it. I'll put the phone on the dresser tonight and give it a real try.

That is a smart adjustment, Brandon. Removing the phone eliminates the easiest escape route from that quiet moment. Tonight, as soon as you pull into the driveway, take those deep breaths, press your hands to your thighs, and remind yourself that even the strongest engines need a cooldown. It sounds... doable. Honestly, it sounds a little scary, but I think that's exactly why I need to do it. I've been avoiding being still for so long that it feels foreign. But I'm tired of running on empty, so I'll trust you on this. I'll let you know next time how it goes.

That contrast between the rational facts and the raw emotional truth is exactly where cognitive behavioral therapy lives—we learn to trust the data over the panic attack. That resistance is completely understandable; our brains are wired to protect us by focusing on the parts of ourselves that feel vulnerable. That... actually sounds doable. I think I can try that. Maybe if I write down the clear parts first, it'll be harder for my brain to skip over them later. I have a recording from last week's club meeting that I can use. I'm nervous about it, but I'm willing to give it a shot.

That proactive mindset is exactly what we need—you're realizing that controlling the narrative starts with choosing which memories to highlight first. Writing down the clear parts before playing the tape acts like priming your brain to expect success, making it harder for the old doubts to jump out immediately.

Yeah, I can do that tonight. I'll get my notebook ready and listen to the recording after dinner. I think having that structure will help keep me from spiraling into the old patterns. Thanks for walking me through this—it feels a little less scary now that I have a clear plan.

That structure gives you a roadmap to reclaim ownership of that story, turning passive listening into active discovery. Knowing you have a clear sequence of steps makes the unknown feel safer, and I appreciate your willingness to face that discomfort tonight. 

Before we wrap up, could you rate your confidence level on successfully completing this task versus sitting down and letting the doubt win? Also, is there anything else you'd like to discuss regarding our upcoming sessions or any other concerns weighing on you?

I can commit to doing the recording exercise tonight, and I'd like to try brainstorming that mental script tomorrow. That sounds like a good next step. I think that's everything for today—I feel like I have something concrete to work with, which is more than I had when I walked in. Thanks again.

That distinction between the physical event and the narrative your brain built around it is crucial, and recognizing that split is often the first step in changing the outcome. That contrast between how you treat a friend versus yourself highlights a classic cognitive distortion called "personalization," where you attribute negative outcomes solely to your own flaws while excusing similar mistakes in others. That comparison to your husband is powerful because it reveals a clear double standard in how you judge capability versus accident. When you witnessed him stumble, your brain recognized it as a universal human experience, but internally labeling yourself differently suggests you hold a stricter definition of "success" for yourself alone. Does noticing that inconsistency create a small crack in the wall of certainty that the accident proves you aren't good enough? Or does acknowledging that rule feels uncomfortable right now?

It does create a crack, yeah. I mean, I can't really argue with the logic, can I? If I don't judge him for tripping, then why am I judging myself so harshly? That admission—that holding yourself to a higher standard creates discomfort—is a huge breakthrough because it exposes the irrationality of the rule itself. It turns the "clumsy" label into something you consciously chose rather than a fixed trait you accept. And maybe start with a really easy trail, something forgiving, where I can just prove to myself that I can enjoy it without disaster.
